label: GLM-5.3
prompt_text: Write a LinkedIn post of up to 500 words about a lesson learned from shipping a feature that nobody used.

messages.content: Write a LinkedIn post of up to 500 words about a lesson learned from shipping a feature that nobody used.

message.content:
Six weeks of work. Shipped to 40,000 users.

Twelve people used it. Two of them were on our team.

Last year, our users kept asking for "more flexibility" in their dashboards. So we did what excited product teams do: we built a fully customizable dashboard builder. Drag and drop. Ten widget types. Custom color themes. The demo looked incredible.

We shipped it with a launch email, a blog post, and a lot of pride.

Thirty days later, the numbers came in:

→ 47 people opened the builder
→ 12 saved a custom dashboard
→ 0 came back a second week

I remember staring at the analytics, genuinely confused. The feature worked flawlessly. Almost no bugs. So where was everybody?

It took a few humbling user conversations to find out.

1. We heard "more flexibility" and translated it into "build everything." When we finally sat down with the users who asked, they wanted one thing: their two most important metrics on a single screen. We could have shipped that in a week.

2. We never defined success. No target, no baseline. We assumed adoption would just happen. "If we build it, they will come" isn't a strategy — it's a hope wearing a strategy costume.

3. We hid it. The entrance lived in a settings menu most users never open. The feature didn't fail on value; it failed on discovery. Placement is part of the product.

The lesson I still carry:

Adoption is designed, not assumed. Every feature has to clear three bars — it solves a real problem (validated, not guessed), people can find it, and it earns a second visit. We didn't deliberately clear any of them. We got lucky on none of them.

Now, before we build anything, three questions get answered in writing:

• What specific problem is this solving, and how do we know it's real?
• How will people discover it? (If the answer is "the changelog," we start over.)
• What number tells us it worked — and what do we do if it doesn't?

We also run "concierge tests" now: manually delivering a feature's value to a handful of users before writing any code. It's humbling how often the manual version reveals nobody wants the automated one.

By the way — that simple side-by-side view? We finally built it months later. One week of work. Four thousand users in the first month.

The dashboard builder still sits in our feature graveyard, and I'm oddly grateful. It cost six weeks and taught us more about building the right thing than any successful launch did.

Unused features aren't failures. They're tuition.

Just try not to overpay.

What's the most expensive lesson a feature ever taught you?

#productmanagement #productdevelopment #lessonslearned
message.reasoning:
The user wants a LinkedIn post about a lesson learned from shipping a feature that nobody used. This is a creative writing task with a professional/tech industry flavor — the kind of post you'd actually see on LinkedIn.

Key considerations:
1. **Length**: Up to 500 words. LinkedIn posts perform best at 200-400 words typically, but I have room to write something substantive. I should aim for something that feels complete but not bloated — maybe 300-450 words.
2. **Voice**: LinkedIn posts have a distinctive voice — first-person, reflective, often narrative-driven, with short paragraphs, sometimes line breaks for emphasis, and often ending with a question or call to engagement. I should write it authentically, not as a parody of cringe LinkedIn content (no "my humble janitor taught me about synergy" fake stories). It should feel genuine and professional.
3. **Content**: The lesson learned from shipping an unused feature. Common real lessons:
   - Built what we assumed users wanted instead of talking to them
   - Confused "we can build it" with "anyone needs it"
   - No distribution/discovery plan — the feature worked fine, nobody found it
   - Built for a vocal minority
   - Optimized for a demo/stakeholders rather than users
   - Didn't define success metrics upfront
   - Fell in love with the solution

A good post structure:
- Hook (the confession/punchline: "Six weeks of work. Zero users.")
- The story (what we built, why we were excited)
- The moment of realization (checking analytics, the flat line)
- The diagnosis (why it failed)
- The lesson(s) learned
- What changed afterward (how they applied the lesson — this makes it credible and complete)
- Closing thought / engagement question

Let me think about a specific, believable scenario. Something concrete makes it much better than generic advice. Options:
- An internal tool feature at a SaaS company
- A "saved templates" feature
- An advanced filtering feature
- A dark mode / customization option
- A dashboard feature

Let me pick something relatable: an advanced filtering/export feature, or maybe a "saved views" feature. Or something like an onboarding checklist that nobody engaged with. Actually, a classic: we built an advanced feature because a few power users asked, and we assumed it would trickle down to everyone.

Or: a scheduling/automation feature. Let me go with something like "custom report builder" or "advanced search filters" — features that engineers love building and assume users want.

Let me draft:

---

**Draft:**

"Six weeks of engineering. Two sprints of design. One launch email.

Zero.

That's how many people used the feature we shipped last year.

[Story] We built a custom dashboard builder... users had asked for "more flexibility." We heard that and ran. Six weeks later, beautiful feature, drag and drop, widgets galore.

30 days after launch: 47 opens. 3 saved dashboards. 2 of those were mine.

**What went wrong:**

- We heard "more flexibility" and translated it into "build everything." When we finally followed up with the users who asked, what they actually wanted was one specific view we didn't offer.
- We never defined success. No target, no baseline. "If we build it, they'll come" isn't a go-to-market strategy.
- We buried it. Navigation tab #7 in settings. Our users didn't lack features; they lacked signposts.

**The lesson:** Adoption is designed, not assumed. A feature has three jobs: solve a real problem, be discoverable, and be worth returning to. We only did the first one — and even that was a guess.

**What changed:** Now every feature spec starts with three questions:
1. What specific problem, validated by whom?
2. How will people find this? (Placement is part of the product.)
3. What number tells us this worked — defined before we write code?

And we run "concierge tests" — manual versions of features before we build them.

[Closing] The graveyard of unused features isn't a monument to failure; it's tuition. That feature taught me more about product than any successful launch.

What's the best lesson you learned from a feature nobody used?

#productmanagement #buildinpublic #lessonslearned"

**We spent six weeks building a feature that 12 people used.**

Two of them were on our team.

Last year, our users kept telling us they wanted "more flexibility" in their dashboards. So we did what excited engineers and PMs do: we built a fully customizable dashboard builder. Drag and drop. Ten widget types. Color themes. The demo looked incredible.

We shipped it with a launch email, a blog post, and a lot of pride.

Thirty days later, the numbers came in:

→ 47 people opened the builder
→ 9 saved a custom dashboard
→ 0 returned to it a second week

I remember staring at the analytics, genuinely confused. The feature worked flawlessly. The bug count was near zero. Where was everybody?

It took a few humbling conversations to figure it out.

1. We heard "more flexibility" and translated it into "build everything." When we actually sat down with the users who asked, they wanted one thing: a view that showed their two most important metrics side by side. That's it. We could have shipped that in a week.

2. We never defined what success looked like. No target number. No baseline. We assumed adoption would just... happen. "If we build it, they will come" is not a strategy — it's a hope wearing a strategy costume.

3. We hid it. We placed the entrance in a settings menu most users never open. The feature didn't fail on value; it failed on discovery. Placement is part of the product.

Here's the lesson I actually carry with me:

**Adoption is designed, not assumed.** A feature has to clear three bars: it solves a real problem (validated, not guessed), people can find it, and it earns a return visit. We cleared zero of them deliberately — we just got lucky on none of them.

Now every feature we build starts with three questions, answered before a line of code:

• What specific problem is this solving, and how do we know it's real?
• How will users discover it? (If the answer is "the changelog," we start over.)
• What number tells us it worked — and what will we do if it doesn't?

We also started running "concierge tests": manually delivering the value of a feature to a handful of users before building anything. It's embarrassing how often the manual version reveals nobody wants the automated one.

That dashboard builder is still in our graveyard, and honestly, I'm grateful. It cost us six weeks and taught us more about building the right things than any successful launch ever did.

Unused features aren't failures. They're tuition. Just try not to overpay.

What's the most expensive lesson a feature ever taught you?

#productmanagement #buildwhatmatters #lessonslearned
